findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Monitoring 2026-2027 and Our Future Council 2.0 - Investing in Our Services
findings.headline: Pay award settlement at 3.3% exceeds 3% budget provision; gap must be funded from contingencies or reserves
findings.detail: Budget included 3% pay provision but national employers offered 3.3% in March 2026, accepted for chief officers in June 2026. Negotiations continue for other pay grades. Any increase above 3% requires funding from corporate contingencies, in-year efficiencies or reserves, with recurrent impact built into future MTFS.
findings.matters: Pay cost overruns reduce available resources; multiple pay grades settling above budget is a material risk to the balanced budget position
findings.figures: 3% budgeted provision; 3.3% settled for chief officers; negotiations ongoing for other grades
findings.quote: the budget includes provision for a 3% pay award. In March 2026 National Employers on behalf of local authorities made a full and final offer of 3.3% for pay award for the 2026-2027 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Monitoring 2026-2027 and Our Future Council 2.0 - Investing in Our Services
findings.headline: DSG deficit of £14.1 million excluded from accounts via statutory override, but override expires 31 March 2028 and government grant coverage unclear
findings.detail: Cumulative DSG deficit of £14.1 million is currently hidden from accounts via statutory override, extended only to 31 March 2028. Government's promised High Needs Stability Grant may cover up to 90% of deficit but eligibility and actual amount remain unknown. Balance would remain with council.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liability; when override ends, if grant doesn't cover full amount, council could face £14.1 million call on reserves or emergency savings mid-MTFS period
findings.figures: £14.1 million cumulative net DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026; statutory override extended to 31 March 2028; High Needs Stability Grant up to 90% of deficit but amount unknown
findings.quote: The cumulative net DSG deficit to 31 March 2026 totalled £14.1 million. The statutory override allowing DSG deficits to be excluded from the Council's wider financial position has been extended to 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Monitoring 2026-2027 and Our Future Council 2.0 - Investing in Our Services
findings.headline: Savings target delivery at risk: some services indicating slippage or non-delivery against £8.4 million 2026-2027 savings target
findings.detail: While majority of services are on track, a small number of the £8.4 million approved savings targets are indicating potential slippage or non-delivery. Council has £3.3 million corporate contingency held to cover shortfalls. Some areas showing overachievement, but delivery remains closely monitored.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver planned savings would immediately worsen the medium-term position and increase reliance on reserves or emergency service cuts
findings.figures: £8.4 million total 2026-2027 savings targets; £3.3 million corporately held contingency for slippage
findings.quote: A small number of these savings targets are indicating some potential slippage or non-delivery. However, early indications also show that in some areas there is potential overachievement of savings delivery.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Monitoring 2026-2027 and Our Future Council 2.0 - Investing in Our Services
findings.headline: Structural budget deficit of £3.8 million forecast for 2027-2028, rising to £14.8 million in 2028-2029, despite improvement from prior projections
findings.detail: Despite progress from Our Future Council programme, the council faces significant medium-term funding gaps. The deficit has improved from £23.5 million modelled the previous year, but a £14.8 million structural shortfall by 2028-2029 signals the council will need to find substantial additional savings or service reductions. This assumes council tax increases to referendum limits.
findings.matters: A £14.8 million structural deficit indicates the current financial model is not yet sustainable and further major service changes or income growth will be required
findings.figures: £3.8 million projected deficit 2027-2028; £14.8 million projected deficit 2028-2029; improvement from £23.5 million previously modelled
findings.quote: the Council is now faced with a projected budget deficit of £3.8 million for 2027-2028 (compared to £23.5 million when modelled in the previous year's budget and MTFS report), rising to £14.8 million in 2028-2029.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Monitoring 2026-2027 and Our Future Council 2.0 - Investing in Our Services
findings.headline: Adult Social Care facing emerging cost pressures from increased demand and care package costs despite £12.5 million additional budget allocation
findings.detail: Early forecasts indicate potential cost pressures within care purchasing budgets due to increased demand and rising care costs. Currently projected to be offset by one-off staffing vacancy savings and income, but this requires continued monitoring with services required to produce recovery plans if pressures persist into the year.
findings.matters: Social care is typically the fastest-growing cost for councils and hardest to control; unmanaged demand pressures here directly threaten financial sustainability
findings.figures: £12.5 million additional budget approved for Adult Social Care in February 2026; emerging pressures currently projected to be offset by one-off savings
findings.quote: Early forecasts indicate some potential cost pressures within care purchasing budgets due to the increased demand and cost of care packages.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Private sector damp-and-mould enforcement requires additional resources that are not secured
findings.detail: Serious complaints about damp and mould in private rentals increased year-on-year through winter 2024-25. Council explicitly states: 'Without additional resource and funding, dealing with serious mould cases cannot be established as a business as usual work stream and the service will continue to respond reactively.' No budget allocation given.
findings.matters: Inability to resource a statutory enforcement function signals either spending pressures or service capacity limits. Reactive-only response to escalating demand is unsustainable.
findings.figures: Risk score 12 (unchanged, target 8); scores increased during winter 2024-2025
findings.quote: Without additional resource and funding, dealing with serious mould cases cannot be established as a 'business as usual' work stream and the service will continue to respond reactively.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Social housing regulator issued C2 rating with noted weaknesses requiring significant remediation
findings.detail: January 2026: Regulator of Social Housing gave the council a C2 grading (no serious failings but weaknesses noted). Regulator specifically flagged 'weaknesses in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards'. Multiple improvement tasks identified requiring 'significant focus'.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance failures in council housing can trigger enforcement action, financial penalties, and reputational damage. The council is managing a large housing stock (8,200+ on waiting list) under regulatory scrutiny.
findings.figures: C2 grading (January 28, 2026); risk score 8 (unchanged, target 8)
findings.quote: On 28 January 2026 the Regulator of Social Housing issued CWC a C2 grading, noting no serious failings, and in line with our self-referral that 'weaknesses in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards'.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Capital projects face cost overrun, timing, and business-case alignment risks
findings.detail: The council acknowledges risks to ongoing capital projects (city centre regeneration, City Learning Quarter) in terms of costs, timings, and whether business cases continue to align with strategy. No quantified budget impacts given.
findings.matters: Capital project delivery risk directly affects council cash flow, borrowing needs, and return on investment. Lenders track whether councils deliver projects to budget.
findings.figures: Risk score 8 (unchanged, target 8)
findings.quote: There are risks to ongoing Council managed and operated capital projects and programmes in terms of costs, timings and ensuring that original business cases continue to align with the Council's strategic aims.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Core financial system migration at risk of missing implementation deadline
findings.detail: The Agresso SaaS migration is flagged as a delivery risk. If implementation slips, the council's core financial systems could be significantly impacted. Risk remains high at 12 with target of 8.
findings.matters: Core financial system stability is essential for managing council operations and financial reporting. A failed migration or missed deadline could disrupt financial controls and reporting.
findings.figures: Risk score 12 (target 8)
findings.quote: There is a risk the Council's Agresso SaaS migration is not successfully implemented in time resulting in the Council's core financial systems being significantly impacted and posing a reputational risk to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Equal pay claims pose unquantified contingent liability
findings.detail: The council faces potential exposure to equal pay claims arising from unapproved local working practices and new case law. No mitigation detail provided; risk score remains at maximum (12) with no improvement in sight.
findings.matters: Equal pay claims are open-ended contingent liabilities that can crystallize unpredictably and absorb significant council resources. Lenders need to understand scale and likelihood.
findings.figures: Risk score 12 (unchanged, target 12)
findings.quote: Due to potential unapproved local working practices, and new case law, there is a risk the Council could be exposed to future equal pay claims, thus impacting Council resources.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Medium-term financial strategy hinges on unknowns over next three years
findings.detail: The council is facing significant uncertainty about future demand for services, inflation, and government policy changes through 2028-2029. This uncertainty is stopping them from developing a robust financial plan. The risk score has improved from 20 to 16, but remains elevated at target 12.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council can plan and manage finances reliably over the term of any loan. Admission of inability to develop a robust strategy is a material concern.
findings.figures: Risk score: 16 (down from 20, target 12); timeframe: three years to 2028-2029
findings.quote: There remains significant uncertainty in relation to demand for services, inflation and the impact of proposed changes to Government Policy, over the period of the MTFS, that being the next three years to 2028-2029. This uncertainty creates a risk that we cannot develop a robust medium term financial strategy.

findings.figures: Amber for both 2026-2027 and MTFS period
findings.quote: The risk of successful appeals against business rates.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) Risk Register
findings.headline: Savings delivery risk: non-delivery of approved savings targets rated Amber for both periods
findings.detail: The register identifies ongoing risk of delays or non-delivery of approved savings targets, rated Amber for both 2026-2027 and the MTFS period, indicating this is a sustained concern.
findings.matters: Budget delivery dependent on savings that may not materialise creates unplanned deficit risk if targets are missed.
findings.figures: Amber for 2026-2027; Amber for MTFS period
findings.quote: Risks that might materialise as a result of delays / non delivery of approved savings targets.

findings.headline: Statutory service demand pressures in social care and temporary accommodation rated Red for MTFS period
findings.detail: Demand risks for statutory services are rated Amber for 2026-2027 but Red for MTFS period. The register specifically names adults and children's social care and temporary accommodation as areas where demand might outstrip resources.
findings.matters: These are historically the largest budget risks in English councils; Red-rated demand for these services signals the council expects serious pressures in 2027-2029.
findings.quote: Risks that might materialise as a result of demands for statutory services outstretching the available resources. This particularly applies to adults and children's social care, and temporary accommodation.

findings.headline: MTFS period to 2028-2029 rated Red due to demand, inflation and funding uncertainty
findings.detail: The council's medium-term financial outlook faces a Red risk rating, with the register explicitly stating this is mainly due to increased demand, inflation costs and uncertainty around future funding. This contrasts with 2026-2027 which is Amber.
findings.matters: A Red MTFS rating indicates the council expects material budget viability risks to materialise in 2027-2029, which directly affects lending risk and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: MTFS 2028-2029 rated Red; 2026-2027 rated Amber
findings.quote: as reported to Cabinet in February 2026 the overall level of risks associated with Medium Term Financial Strategy up to 2028-2029 is currently assessed as Red mainly due to risks which might materialise as a result of increased demand, inflation costs and due to uncertainty around future funding.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management - Annual Report 2025-2026 and Activity Monitoring Quarter One 2026-2027
findings.headline: Service investment elements of prudential indicators forecast to exceed approved limits for 2027-2029.
findings.detail: The report flags that service investment components within the council's authorised limit and operational boundary are forecast to exceed the best estimates approved in February 2026. This is attributed to rephasing of capital programmes across years. While the overall limits remain within approved ceilings, the service investment component alone exceeds forecast. The council will review and re-set these limits at the next budget cycle.
findings.matters: Prudential indicators are self-imposed borrowing limits designed to ensure prudence. Exceeding forecasted components — even if within overall ceilings — suggests the council's capital planning visibility or control is tighter than current forecasts allow. A lender watches whether councils stay within their own self-determined limits, as drift signals loss of control.
findings.figures: Service investment elements forecast to slightly exceed best estimates for 2028-2029 (authorised limit) and 2027-2028 and 2028-2029 (operational boundary)
findings.quote: with regards 'PI 3 – Authorised limit for external debt' the forecast for 2028-2029 for service investments is slightly in excess of the best estimate presented to Council in the Treasury Management Strategy in February 2026. Likewise, 'PI 4 – Operational boundary for external debt' is in a similar position for service investments in 2027-2028 and 2028-2029.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management - Annual Report 2025-2026 and Activity Monitoring Quarter One 2026-2027
findings.headline: Three LOBO loans were called and rejected as lenders offered penalty rates; council managing debt in stressed market.
findings.detail: During 2025-2026, three Lender Option Borrower Option loans totalling £17 million were called. Lenders offered new rates ranging from 6.19% to 6.26%, significantly above the loans' current rates (3.60% to 4.29%). Wolverhampton rejected all proposals and repaid the loans instead. This shows the council is watchful for lender opportunism but also signals the debt refinancing market is becoming challenging.
findings.matters: LOBO calls with punitive rates are a stress signal in the public debt market. A lender to the council needs to understand that refinancing older borrowing is becoming more expensive and that the council is actively managing to avoid being trapped into higher rates. This affects future borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £17.0 million total LOBO principal called; proposed rates 6.19%, 6.21%, 6.26% versus current rates of 3.60%, 4.26%, 4.29%
findings.quote: Due to current market conditions some LOBO lenders are 'calling' their options and offering inflated long term rates deliberately set unattractively high so it would not be accepted. In order to be prudent, the potential for these 'calls' are included in the Council's cashflow projections to ensure that if called, the Council are in a position to repay the loans to avoid these higher rates.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management - Annual Report 2025-2026 and Activity Monitoring Quarter One 2026-2027
findings.headline: Capital programme financing requirement grew £42.3 million in one year, with HRA borrowing need surging.
findings.detail: The council's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes increased from £1,109.9 million to £1,152.2 million during 2025-2026. The split shifted: HRA (housing) borrowing need grew £63.5 million while General Fund fell £21.2 million. This means more of future borrowing will service housing rather than general services.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what's driving borrowing growth. This shows the council's capital programme — particularly housing — is larger than originally forecast and will require proportionally more HRA revenue to service. HRA borrowing ratios and housing schemes carrying their own borrowing risk matter to credit analysis.
findings.figures: CFR increased £42.3 million (1,109.9 to 1,152.2); HRA CFR up £63.5 million; General Fund CFR down £21.2 million
findings.quote: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) increased from £1,109.9 million to £1,152.2 million throughout 2025-2026. This reflects a net increase in the Council's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes of £42.3 million. This was split between the General Fund and HRA at a rate of 56% and 44% respectively.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management - Annual Report 2025-2026 and Activity Monitoring Quarter One 2026-2027
findings.headline: Council secured £20 million-plus long-term saving through debt rescheduling.
findings.detail: Wolverhampton repaid £55.8 million of fixed market debt held with Barclays at a discount during 2025-2026. The refinancing is projected to deliver savings in excess of £20 million over the next 40 years. This was a material opportunity captured during the year.
findings.matters: A lender tracking council financial health looks for evidence of prudent debt management and active refinancing to control long-term interest costs. This shows Wolverhampton is watching its debt portfolio and acting opportunistically.
findings.figures: £55.8 million repaid; projected savings over £20.0 million over the next 40 years
findings.quote: A debt rescheduling opportunity was undertaken during the year, repaying the fixed market debt of £55.8 million held with Barclays at a discount, which is projected to result in potential savings of over £20.0 million over the next 40 years.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Capital programme rated as amber risk overall, with strategic MTFS risk from demand uncertainty and government funding volatility
findings.detail: The council's Strategic Risk Register continues to rate the overall capital programme risk as amber. The primary driver is uncertainty in the Medium Term Financial Strategy around demand for services, inflation, and levels of government funding—the same funding sources the capital programme depends on.
findings.matters: Amber risk rating on capital combined with acknowledged MTFS uncertainty signals management concern about both programme delivery and the funding environment; this constrains the council's financial resilience
findings.figures: £396m total borrowing planned; 66.1% of capital dependent on government grants
findings.quote: The overall risk associated with the programme continues to be quantified as amber.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Two-thirds of capital funding is dependent on bid-reliant external grants with single-year settlements
findings.detail: 66.1% of the General Fund capital programme (£275.9m of £417.4m) is funded by external resources, predominantly single-year grants from central government and the West Midlands Combined Authority. The council notes this reliance and the bid-dependent nature contributes to programme profile uncertainty.
findings.matters: Heavy dependency on bid-reliant, single-year grant funding creates significant downside risk; if grant applications fail or funding is delayed, the council has limited internal resources to substitute and may have to cut capital delivery or increase borrowing
findings.figures: External resources 66.1% of General Fund capital financing; £269.5m of programme initially funded externally, increased to £275.9m in latest forecast
findings.quote: As the external resources, most significantly grants from central government and the WMCA, represent 66.1% of budget financing, the prevalence of single-year funding settlements and bid-reliant applications for funding also contributes to this profile.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Capital delivery underperformed in 2025-2026, with 21% of General Fund budget re-profiled to future years
findings.detail: General Fund capital delivery reached only 79.1% of approved budget (£70.2m spent of £88.8m approved), with £18.6m re-profiled into later years in line with financial challenge priorities. This shows execution risk against the planned capital programme.
findings.matters: Persistent capital slippage affects the council's ability to deliver planned projects on time and can signal project management or resource constraints; re-profiling also defers income generation from capital assets
findings.figures: 2025-2026 General Fund: £70.2m outturn vs £88.8m approved = 79.1% delivery; £18.6m re-profiled
findings.quote: The outturn 2025-2026 expenditure for existing General Fund capital investment projects totals £70.2 million, representing delivery of the investment programme at 79.1% against the approved budget of £88.8 million.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Asset maintenance contingency is insufficient for full replacement costs
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that the Corporate Provision and Contingency for Future Programmes budget is inadequate to fund the full extent of costs needed for maintaining and replacing council assets, even after asset rationalisation efforts.
findings.matters: Insufficient contingency to cover asset maintenance suggests a deteriorating asset base, future unfunded liabilities, and heightened risk of emergency capital calls or service-affecting deferrals
findings.figures: Total capital programme: £417.4m General Fund + £577.8m HRA
findings.quote: However, it should be noted that this resource is not sufficient to fund the full extent of the potential costs of maintaining and replacing our assets.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Construction cost pressures are already realising and impacting capital project budgets
findings.detail: The council reports that rising construction costs in materials, labour and supply chain disruptions are actively impacting project budgets now, not just as a future risk. The council acknowledges significant uncertainty remains about future cost pressures and is monitoring their ongoing impact.
findings.matters: Materialising cost pressures on a £396m borrowing programme could lead to overspends, delivery delays, and reduced financial flexibility to manage the capital programme within budgeted borrowing
findings.figures: Increases in material costs already being realised; £102.8m General Fund borrowing plus £293.5m HRA borrowing planned through 2030-2031
findings.quote: There remains significant uncertainty and cost pressures which continue to affect the capital investment programme. Rising construction costs – particularly in materials, labour and supply chain disruptions – are already impacting project budgets.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Council is under financial stress and restructuring capital delivery to find revenue savings
findings.detail: Wolverhampton established its 'Our Future Council' programme in November 2024 explicitly 'in recognition of the extent of the financial challenge the Council faces'. The capital programme is being reviewed to identify opportunities to generate revenue budget savings (noted twice in the recommendations). Asset rationalisation is being used to reduce costs and generate capital receipts.
findings.matters: A council restructuring its capital and revenue delivery due to financial challenges signals constrained financial position and raises questions about the ability to service increased debt
findings.figures: £396m total prudential borrowing planned (£102.8m General Fund + £293.5m HRA through 2030-2031)
findings.quote: In November 2024, Cabinet approved the approach and guiding principles of Our Future Council (OFC) in recognition of the extent of the financial challenge the Council faces.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Assessment of Going Concern
findings.headline: Capital investment programme experiencing cost inflation and supply chain pressure
findings.detail: The council's multi-year capital programme (£352.6 million across 2024-25 to 2029-30) faces material cost pressures from construction market conditions. Rising costs in materials, labour, and supply chain disruptions are impacting project budgets. The council monitors but has not published mitigation.
findings.matters: Multi-year capital commitments can significantly impact future revenue if projects overrun or require accelerated borrowing. Sustained cost inflation in the construction sector could force repricing or deferral of planned investment.
findings.figures: Medium-term capital programme £352.6 million (2024-25 to 2029-30); 2025-2026 outturn £70.2 million against revised budget £87.1 million
findings.quote: There remains significant uncertainty and cost pressures which continue to affect the capital investment programme. Rising construction costs, particularly in materials, labour and supply chain disruptions are impacting on project budgets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Assessment of Going Concern
findings.headline: Children's social care cost growth is explicitly flagged as a particular challenge
findings.detail: Among medium-term pressures facing the council (including pay inflation and general demand growth), increases in children's social care costs are specifically identified as a particular challenge. The council also faces increased demand pressures in adult social care.
findings.matters: Children's social care is demand-driven, difficult to control, and a known area of overspend across councils. Its specific callout here suggests the council views it as a material risk that may continue to drive budget pressures despite savings plans.
findings.figures: 2026-2027 budget £396.2 million; savings targets £8.4 million
findings.quote: Like many other local authorities, the Council continues to be faced with pressures over the medium term, such as pay and other inflationary related pressures, increases in costs within children's social care being a particular challenge.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Assessment of Going Concern
findings.headline: Medium-term deficit projections improved significantly after funding settlement, but deficits remain forecast for 2027-2028 and 2028-2029
findings.detail: In February 2025, the council projected a £23.5 million deficit for 2027-2028. Following the February 2026 funding settlement (Fair Funding Review), this projection improved to £3.8 million for the same year, though it then rises to £14.8 million by 2028-2029. This material improvement in outlook reflects changes to central government funding allocation favouring higher-deprivation councils.
findings.matters: Lenders assess councils' medium-term sustainability through multi-year projections. The improvement is positive but the remaining deficits show continued financial challenges that must be managed through delivery of the council's Our Future Council savings programme.
findings.figures: 2027-2028 deficit: £23.5 million (Feb 2025 projection) reduced to £3.8 million (Feb 2026 projection); 2028-2029 projected deficit £14.8 million
findings.quote: In February 2026, it was reported that the updated projected budget deficit was £3.8 million for 2027-2028 (compared to £23.5 million previously), rising to £14.8 million by 2028-2029.

findings.paper_title: Final Audit and Risk Committee Report - Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026
findings.headline: All 17 Financial Management Code standards now assessed as green after improvement of one previously amber standard
findings.detail: The Council conducted a self-assessment against CIPFA's 17 Financial Management Code standards. One standard that was previously assessed as amber (requiring improvement) has been reviewed and updated. That standard has now moved to green, meaning all 17 standards are now assessed as green, demonstrating full compliance.
findings.matters: The Financial Management Code is a formal framework designed to identify risks to financial sustainability and demonstrates the council's compliance with standards for good financial management practice.
findings.figures: All 17 standards now green (previously 16 green, 1 amber)
findings.quote: This standard have been reviewed and updated, which have resulted in the final standard moving from amber to green. This has resulted in all 17 standards now assessed as green.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Reserves
findings.headline: Future Years Budget Strategy Reserve held with £2m already committed for forward spending
findings.detail: The council holds £7.6m in this reserve specifically to 'support the budget strategy in future years,' with £2m already approved for commitment. This indicates the council expects budget pressures ahead and is building a specific buffer to manage them.
findings.matters: Deliberate provisioning for future budget gaps suggests the council anticipates structural pressures; reliance on reserves rather than in-year solutions may limit flexibility.
findings.figures: Future Years Budget Strategy Reserve: £7,602k total; Approved commitments: £2,000k
findings.quote: Funds available to support the budget strategy in future years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Reserves
findings.headline: Schools balances drawn down by £4.4m in year, leaving £11.7m
findings.detail: Schools balances fell from £13.4m to £11.7m with a transfer out of £4.4m. This represents significant drawdown from what may be a key buffer against rising school spending pressures, particularly given national cost pressures in education.
findings.matters: Declining school reserves can signal emerging cost pressures or planned spending; if schools are using reserves to balance budgets, this reduces future flexibility.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Reserves
findings.headline: Enterprise Zone Business Rates Reserve of £5.5m marked as pending business case approval
findings.detail: The reserve grew from £2.95m to £5.46m with £2.5m added in-year, but the council explicitly notes this is 'pending drawdown for committed activity which is subject to business case approval.' This creates uncertainty about whether this £5.5m will actually be deployed and when.
findings.matters: Lenders need clarity on whether business rates income is committed or contingent; reserves held pending approval suggest uncertainty in an already volatile revenue source.

findings.quote: Funds transferred in to be held pending drawdown for committed activity which is subject to business case approval

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Reserves
findings.headline: Council adding £8m to transformation and investment reserves in single year

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Outturn 2025-2026 and Reserves and Provisions 2025-2026
findings.headline: Homelessness placements collapsed to 64 families in Q4 from 121 in Q3, with average time in temporary accommodation at 149 days.
findings.detail: The number of families successfully moved into secure housing fell sharply from 121 in Q3 to 64 in Q4 2025-2026. The council attributes this to constraints in property availability and shortage of suitable move-on options, not reduced demand. Time spent in temporary accommodation remains high at 149 days average, indicating households are spending extended periods in temporary housing.
findings.matters: A sharp quarterly collapse in homelessness placements indicates a structural shortage of available housing and move-on options that the council cannot resolve. This represents an unfunded statutory duty and potential pressure on housing and temporary accommodation budgets, with possible implications for other council services.
findings.figures: 121 families placed in Q3; 64 families placed in Q4 (47% drop); 149 days average time in temporary accommodation
findings.quote: Homelessness outcomes are showing signs of deterioration, with the number of families moved into secure housing falling from 121 in Q3 to 64 by the end of Q4, despite higher levels earlier in the year (peaking at 140 in Q2 2025-2026). This decline reflects ongoing constraints in property availability, rather than reduced demand, alongside a shortage of suitable move‑on options within the system.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Outturn 2025-2026 and Reserves and Provisions 2025-2026
findings.headline: Parking income shortfall creating £732,000 overspend, indicating possible weakness in city centre footfall or changed travel patterns.
findings.detail: Parking services is reporting a £732,000 overspend comprised of income shortfall, additional operating costs, and pressures within parking enforcement. The combination of lower income alongside cost growth is a negative indicator for a service expected to contribute positively to general fund.
findings.matters: Parking income shortfalls often signal reduced city centre vitality, lower commuter footfall, or changed transport patterns. This trend, combined with rising operating costs, suggests structural economic weakness affecting a key council income source.
findings.figures: £732,000 overspend in parking services
findings.quote: Parking services is also reporting an overspend totalling £732,000 due to a combination of shortfall on income in parking, additional operating costs and pressures within parking enforcement.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Outturn 2025-2026 and Reserves and Provisions 2025-2026
findings.headline: High Needs Block DSG accumulated deficit of £16.4 million, partially dependent on government grant of up to 90% whose level and conditions remain undefined.
findings.detail: The High Needs Block component of Dedicated Schools Grant has accumulated a deficit of £16.4 million by end of March 2026, with an in-year deficit of £10.4 million. The council uses a statutory accounting override to carry this outside the main revenue budget. Government announced in February 2026 a High Needs Stability Grant to assist authorities, with payment due summer 2026 covering up to 90% of the deficit. However, the grant amount depends on government assessment of eligible expenditure and local authorities meeting undefined conditions, creating uncertainty.
findings.matters: A £16.4 million accumulated deficit represents a contingent liability. While government may cover up to 90%, reliance on government discretion on eligible costs and undefined conditions creates budget uncertainty. If grant is lower than maximum or conditions unmet, the council could face a significant unexpected cost.
findings.figures: £16.4 million accumulated High Needs Block deficit at 31 March 2026; £10.4 million in-year deficit; maximum government grant up to 90% of £14.1 million net position
findings.quote: The High Needs Block of Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) ended 2025-2026 with an in-year deficit of £10.4 million. The total accumulated deficit against the High Needs Block grant is £16.4 million at the end of 2025-2026. Currently for accounting purposes there is a statutory override which means we can carry forward a deficit balance outside of the Council's main revenue budget. In February 2026 Government announced its intention to pay a High Needs Stability Grant to assist local authorities with DSG deficits. The grant is due to be paid in the summer of 2026 which will be up to a maximum value of 90% of the £14.1 million accrued net deficit as at 31 March 2026, recognised in the unusable reserve. The level of grant is currently unknown and will depend on what Government deems to be eligible expenditure and local authorities meeting other conditions.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Outturn 2025-2026 and Reserves and Provisions 2025-2026
findings.headline: Children's social care overspend of £3.4 million in complex placements despite £7.6 million additional budget, with £5.0 million more required for 2026-2027.
findings.detail: The Children and Young People In Care service overspent by £3.4 million in 2025-2026 driven by costs of complex residential and care packages. This occurred despite £7.6 million additional budget being allocated during the year. The council is committing a further £5.0 million for 2026-2027 plus £1.0 million corporate contingency to manage projected demand and cost inflation.
findings.matters: Cost growth in a provider-led market for complex placements is volatile and hard to control. Repeated budget increases failing to prevent overspends suggests the council has limited control over cost growth and faces material risk of further deficits if placements or complexity increase further.
findings.figures: £3.4 million overspend in 2025-2026; £7.6 million additional budget provided in year; £5.0 million additional budget plus £1.0 million contingency committed for 2026-2027
findings.quote: The main pressures are seen in the Children and Young People In Care service totalling £3.4 million due to increased cost of complex residential and care packages including Children with Disabilities and Short Breaks in a provider led market. This is after additional budget of £7.6 million in Children and Young People In Care service to support cost pressures. The 2026-2027 budget incorporates £5.0 million of additional budget to support increases due to demand and cost inflation for care packages with additional budget contingency totalling £1.0 million held corporately.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Delivering Our Services - Performance and Budget Outturn 2025-2026 and Reserves and Provisions 2025-2026
findings.headline: Adult social care overspend of £2.8 million despite £11 million additional budget, with a further £12.5 million committed for 2026-2027.
findings.detail: The Adult Social Care directorate overspent by £2.8 million in 2025-2026 even after receiving £11.0 million additional budget during the year. The overspend is driven by increased demand for care packages and rising complexity of need. The council has pre-committed a further £12.5 million for 2026-2027, indicating the council expects cost pressures to continue escalating.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends despite rising budget allocations signal a structural cost problem that cannot be solved by incremental budget increases alone. A lender would worry about the council's ability to absorb further cost growth or whether reserves are being used to offset ongoing deficits.
findings.figures: £2.8 million overspend (2.41% of £116.2 million budget); £11.0 million additional budget provided in 2025-2026; £12.5 million additional budget allocated for 2026-2027
findings.quote: The Adult Social Care directorate is reporting an outturn overspend of £2.8 million (2.41%) against a net controllable budget of £116.2 million. The overspend mainly relates to increased demand for care packages across Safeguarding and Ageing Well Service and Disabilities and Mental Health Service. This overspend is after additional budget of £11.0 million being incorporated into the 2025-2026 budget. The 2026-2027 Budget incorporates additional budget totalling £12.5 million to support both projected increases in demand and fee uplifts for 2026-2027.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Savings targets profiling was 'ambitious' in February 2025 budget and is now being extended
findings.detail: The council approved £31.8 million in recurrent savings for 2025-2026 to 2027-2028. In the current budget, it acknowledges that 'the profiling and level of some savings targets was ambitious' and is now reprofiling some savings 'over a longer period of time in order that they can be delivered in a more considered way'. It is also removing approximately £1.2 million of originally planned savings. A £2.8 million contingency for slippage/non-delivery exists in 2026-2027, with a further £1.0 million added in November 2025 (though this November addition has now been removed).
findings.matters: Admitting that approved savings were over-ambitious and requiring reprofiling suggests execution risk; councils often miss savings targets
findings.figures: £31.8m recurrent savings approved, ~£1.2m removed, £2.8m contingency for slippage
findings.quote: It was recognised that in February 2025, the profiling and level of some savings targets was ambitious. In light of the favourable funding settlement a number of changes are now proposed. This includes reprofiling some approved savings over a longer period of time in order that they can be delivered in a more considered way and thereby lessening the impact on service delivery.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Children's social care requiring additional £2.0 million on top of £4.0 million approved just 12 months earlier
findings.detail: The council approved £4.0 million additional budget in February 2025 for children's social care pressures (complexity of placements in a provider-led market). It now requires a further £2.0 million in 2026-2027, with £1.0 million held corporately and released in-year. Future years have been re-assumed upward. The pattern of repeated upward revisions within 12 months suggests underlying costs are outpacing initial estimates.
findings.matters: Repeated upward revisions to a single service budget after such short notice suggests cost control is inadequate or demand has fundamentally changed
findings.figures: £4.0m approved Feb 2025, additional £2.0m required (£1.0m held corporately)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Government Social Care Fair Pay Policy (2028-2029 rollout) costs unquantified but included in MTFS
findings.detail: Government is consulting on a Social Care Fair Pay Policy including a national pay agreement, legally enforceable conditions, and annual collective bargaining, rolling out 2028-2029. The council has 'made some high level assumptions and have incorporated these into the medium-term financial strategy' but explicitly flags these as 'early high level indicative projections and will be subject to change'. Government response expected Spring 2026; the council cannot yet quantify the impact or whether additional funding will cover it.
findings.matters: A new national pay floor for social care could materially increase costs; the council has signalled it cannot quantify this risk, indicating exposure to a material unplanned cost
findings.figures: Roll-out 2028-29; costs unspecified
findings.quote: However, in order to be prudent we have made some high level assumptions and have incorporated these into the medium-term financial strategy. These are however, early high level indicative projections and will be subject to change. Updates will be provided to Councillors in future reports.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Council required to use £2.0 million from reserves and capital receipts to balance 2026-2027 budget
findings.detail: The council must draw £2.0 million of one-off resources (capital receipts or earmarked reserves) to fund transformation and balance the 2026-2027 budget. Separately, £11.4 million in prior-year one-off items are reversing: including £5.0 million in capital receipts, £1.703 million in one-off grants, and £1.2 million in dividends. The council states its 'ultimate aim' is to 'remove the reliance on earmarked reserves to balance the budget', but this has not yet been achieved.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance a recurrent budget is unsustainable; it indicates core revenue cannot fund core spending and the council is consuming its financial buffer
findings.figures: £2.0m required 2026-27, £11.4m reversal of prior one-offs (£5.0m receipts, £1.703m grants, £1.2m dividends)
findings.quote: the Council is required to use £2.0 million of one-off resources (earmarked reserves / capital receipts) in order to fund transformation activity and balance the budget for 2026-2027

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: High Needs Block DSG deficit of £6.0 million reported for the first time in 2024-2025
findings.detail: The council reported a £6.0 million deficit on the High Needs Block (SEND funding) for the first time, with a total DSG deficit of £4.9 million. A statutory override allows this to be held on the balance sheet until March 2028, masking cash impact. Government will cover 90% of historic deficits via a High Needs Stability Grant from 2026-2027 (subject to a SEND reform plan), but the council is assuming a further £2.0 million cost pressure in 2028-2029. This suggests the underlying deficit is unresolved and will recur once the override ends.
findings.matters: A first-time deficit of this scale in education funding signals a structural problem; the statutory override mechanism expires March 2028 and provides false comfort about the sustainability of SEND spending
findings.figures: £6.0m High Needs Block deficit (2024-25), £4.9m total DSG deficit, £2.0m projected cost pressure (2028-29)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Pay award for 2026-2027 unresolved, with every 1% above the 3% assumption creating £2 million annual cost
findings.detail: The council's budget assumes 3% for 2026-2027 and 2.5% thereafter, but the actual award remains unagreed. Any overshoot would require funding from 'corporate contingencies, in-year efficiencies and reserves' or would increase the projected deficit. The sensitivity is acute: each percentage point above assumption = £2.0 million per annum, and this sensitivity compounds across the workforce.
findings.matters: Public sector pay typically settles above initial assumptions; this sensitivity suggests the council has minimal budget flexibility to absorb realistic pay outcomes
findings.quote: At the time of writing this report the pay award for 2026-2027 has not been agreed. Our budget proposals, assume that the pay award will be 3% in 2026-2027, and 2.5% in 2027-2028 and 2028-2029... For every 1% increase in pay award costs, there is an additional budget pressure of circa £2.0 million per annum.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Key Assumptions for Budget Pressures and Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Adult social care costs rising to £12.5 million pressure in 2026-2027, up from £10.0 million previously assumed
findings.detail: The council identified £8.0 million in costs from proposed care provider fee uplifts and demographic growth, plus £4.5 million in in-year pressures from 2025-2026. Future projections show £13.0 million (2027-28) and £14.0 million (2028-29). The council notes it is 'confident that with a combination of the additional budget mentioned above, the impact of the 2026-2027 pay award (which is currently held corporately), along with the corporate contingency held to support any in-year pressures within Adult Social Care we will remain above our notional target', but this requires drawing on contingencies.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically a council's largest controllable cost; repeated upward revisions within a single budget cycle suggest demand is outpacing funding and cost control is weak
findings.quote: The estimated cost of the proposed fee uplift along with assumptions around demographic growth are projected to cost circa £8.0 million. In addition, we are also seeing in-year (2025-2026) pressures and the projected impact for 2026-2027 is forecast to be a further £4.5 million, giving a total projected cost pressure of £12.5 million for 2026-2027.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Service and commercial investment debt forecast to peak at 63.9% loan-to-value in 2027-28
findings.detail: Net debt for service/commercial investments (WV Living, Help to Own, investment properties) rises from £30.7m (2025-26) to £41.3m (2027-28), with loan-to-value ratio increasing from 57.3% to peak at 63.9%. Council acknowledges downside risk: if asset fair value falls below borrowing level, Strategic Executive Board would need to reassess whether investments deliver strategic objectives. Investment returns are declining; income falls from 1.5% to 0.9% of net service expenditure.
findings.matters: Rising leverage on commercial assets, combined with council's explicit risk acknowledgment, creates potential for covenant pressure or forced asset sales if valuations decline. Falling investment returns suggest expected returns not materializing.
findings.figures: Net debt £30.7m (2025-26) to £41.3m (2027-28); loan-to-value 57.3% rising to 63.9% (2027-28); investment income 1.5% declining to 0.9% of net service expenditure
findings.quote: In the event that the fair value of the investment is no longer sufficient to provide security against the loss the Strategic Executive Board will need to consider whether the investment is enabling wider strategic objectives.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Investment Strategy
findings.headline: General Fund capital programme assumes £43.5m in capital receipts from planned asset disposals
findings.detail: Council plans significant asset rationalization to generate capital receipts and reduce costs. £43.5m in capital receipts is assumed across the five-year programme (2025-26 to 2030-31). The council requires detailed review of disposal schedules 'to identify only those that are likely to be completed,' indicating execution risk around meeting the receipts target.
findings.matters: Asset sales are volatile funding source. Large assumed receipts create financing risk if disposals don't materialize; failure to achieve target would require capital programme cuts or increased borrowing.
findings.figures: £43.5 million capital receipts assumed over five years (2025-26 to 2030-31)
findings.quote: Capital receipts totalling £43.5 million have been assumed within the General Fund capital investment programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Council pursuing major restructuring through 'Our Future Council' in response to acknowledged financial challenges
findings.detail: In November 2024, Cabinet approved Our Future Council (OFC), explicitly recognizing significant financial challenges. OFC includes asset rationalization to generate capital receipts, becoming 'funder of last resort,' and prudent borrowing only. Strategic Asset Plan is being refreshed to align with OFC principles, with new plan implementation scheduled for 2026.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether a council facing financial stress has board-level recognition and response strategy. OFC being approved and guiding capital planning indicates material financial challenge requiring structural reform.
findings.figures: November 2024 approval; new asset plan for 2026 implementation
findings.quote: In November 2024, Cabinet approved the approach and guiding principles of Our Future Council (OFC) in recognition of the extent of the financial challenge the Council faces.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: Our Future Council savings programme is delivering but carries ongoing execution risk; £2.5m of £25.2m approved savings at risk in 2025-2026

External audit has noted 'improved arrangements in place to identify and report against savings delivery'. The 2026-2027 budget incorporates only £8.4m of new savings, down from previous larger programmes. Corporate contingency is held against delivery slippage.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: External audit delivered clean opinion but flagged financial resilience as ongoing concern
findings.detail: In January 2026, the council received an unqualified audit opinion on accounts and external auditors reported no significant weaknesses in financial sustainability, governance or VFM. However, auditors raised two recommendations specifically under financial sustainability: on Dedicated School Grant and on financial plans over short and medium term to manage financial resilience risk. Both are acknowledged by council and in the Strategic Risk Register.
findings.matters: While the clean audit opinion is reassuring, the auditor's specific concerns about DSG and financial resilience planning suggest these are known vulnerabilities; DSG deficits are a widespread sector issue that can create balance sheet pressure.
findings.figures: Unqualified audit opinion; 2 financial sustainability recommendations raised
findings.quote: External Audit raised only two improvement recommendations under financial sustainability in respect of Dedicated School Grant and financial plans in place over the short and medium term to manage the risk of financial resilience. findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: Budget still relies on £2m of one-off resources (reserves/capital receipts) despite overall balance claim
findings.detail: Although the paper describes 2026-2027 as 'a balanced budget', it requires £2.0m of one-off resources (earmarked reserves or capital receipts) to balance it. This is an improvement on 2025-2026 (£5m), but the Section 151 Officer explicitly states this 'is not a sustainable solution to the Council's underlying medium term estimated financial gap'. One-off resources can only smooth, not solve.
findings.matters: One-off resource use signals underlying budget deficit is not covered by recurring income; even at £2m per year this depletes reserves (current uncommitted earmarked reserves £32.6m) and is unsustainable beyond the near term.
findings.figures: £2.0m one-off resources required in 2026-2027; uncommitted earmarked reserves £32.6m
findings.quote: In the opinion of the Section 151 Officer, the proposed use of earmarked reserves during 2026-2027 is prudent, proportionate and in line with the approved budget strategy for 2026-2027, however, this is not an ongoing sustainable solution to the Council's underlying medium financial challenge

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: Pay award assumption of 3% carries material unfunded risk: each 1% above costs £2m per annum
findings.detail: The budget assumes a 3% pay award for 2026-2027 (actual award not yet known at report date). The paper states that every 1% increase above 3% costs approximately £2m per annum. With no contingency above this rate flagged in the budget narrative, any higher award would need to be funded from corporate contingency (already carrying other risks) or reserves.
findings.matters: Unfunded pay inflation is an immediate P&L hit that cannot be deferred; public sector pay awards are politically difficult to manage down; a 5% award would create a £4m unplanned deficit.
findings.figures: 3% pay award assumed; £2m cost per 1% increase
findings.quote: For every 1% increase in pay award costs, there is an additional budget pressure of circa £2.0 million per annum. Any increase above the 3% currently built into the budget for 2026-2027 would need to be funded from a combination of corporate contingencies, in-year efficiencies and reserves

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: Overall budget risk remains RED despite improvements; material uncertainty from 2028-2029 due to government policy changes
findings.detail: Despite the improved deficit position, the Section 151 Officer maintains a RED risk rating for the MTFS, citing medium-term forecasting risks, service demand risks (particularly social care), and potential cost implications from government policy changes (SEND accounting override end, Social Care Fair Pay Policy, UK Emissions Trading Scheme from 2028). The paper explicitly states these policy impacts are uncertain in quantum.
findings.matters: A RED risk rating on a three-year strategy signals that management do not consider the forecasts robust beyond 2026-2027; unknown government policy costs from 2028 create contingent liabilities that don't yet have provisions.
findings.figures: Overall risk rated RED; Government policy changes create uncertainties from 2028-2029
findings.quote: The overall level of risk associated with the Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029 continues to be assessed as Red. Further action is therefore required to reduce costs and the work of Our Future Council (of transformation and cost reduction) needs to continue

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029
findings.headline: Adult social care costs escalating: £12.5m additional budget pressure identified for 2026-2027 alone
findings.detail: The paper projects £12.5m of additional pressure in adult social care for 2026-2027 (£8m from proposed provider fee uplift plus demographic growth, plus £4.5m in-year pressure). Children's social care budget is also being increased from £4m to £6m. These are recurrent ongoing costs, not one-off, and will compound across the MTFS period.
findings.matters: Growing statutory service obligations (social care is undefeasible) create structural budget pressure that cannot be cut without service failure; a lender needs to know if this trajectory can be sustained through the lending term.

findings.quote: The estimated cost of the proposed fee uplift along with assumptions around demographic growth are projected to cost circa £8.0 million. findings.paper_title: Our Future Council - Investing in Our Services - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2028-2029

The favorable funding settlement (9% increase vs 6.1% nationally) is the primary driver. However, from 2028-2029 onwards the Council remains dependent on identifying new savings, and significant uncertainty persists around government policy changes.
findings.matters: The narrowing deficits materially improve the council's creditworthiness, but uncertainty from 2028 and reliance on continued policy assumptions creates refinancing risk beyond the settlement period.
findings.figures: £3.8m deficit 2027-2028 (vs £23.5m previously), £14.8m 2028-2029 (vs £30m+), core spending power up 9.0% in 2026-2027 and 24.3% by 2028-2029

findings.paper_title: Appendix 11 - Section 25 Statement
findings.headline: One-off reserves being used to balance 2026-2027 budget, explicitly described as unsustainable
findings.detail: The council requires £2.0 million of earmarked reserves and capital receipts to balance the 2026-2027 budget. The Section 151 Officer explicitly states this approach 'is not a sustainable solution to the Council's underlying medium term estimated financial gap'. This indicates the council is masking structural budget problems rather than resolving them.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness needs to know whether reserves are being drawn down to address genuine one-off costs or to defer structural deficit issues that will eventually require either major savings or deteriorating financial metrics.
findings.figures: £2.0 million of one-off resources (earmarked reserves/capital receipts)
findings.quote: the proposed use of earmarked reserves during 2026-2027 is prudent and proportionate for 2026-2027, but that this is not a sustainable solution to the Council's underlying medium term estimated financial gap to 2028-2029

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - 2026-2027 Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: General Fund debt repayment costs (MRP) forecast to increase from £22.4m to £24.5m
findings.detail: General Fund MRP is £22.4 million for 2026-27, rising to £24.5 million in 2027-28—a £2.1 million year-on-year increase of 9.4%. HRA MRP remains flat at £440,000. The Section 151 Officer considers this approach prudent and these charges are incorporated into both treasury and HRA budgets.
findings.matters: Rising MRP reflects growing debt repayment burden from past capital borrowing, reducing revenue budget capacity. The trajectory shows increasing strain on the council's debt sustainability position over time.
findings.figures: £22.4 million for 2026-2027, increasing to £24.5 million in 2027-2028
findings.quote: The forecast General Fund MRP charge would be £22.4 million for 2026-2027, increasing to £24.5 million in 2027-2028.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - 2026-2027 Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Council acknowledges extent of financial challenge, driving strategic asset rationalisation through Our Future Council
findings.detail: In November 2024 Cabinet approved the Our Future Council approach in recognition of what the report explicitly describes as 'the extent of the financial challenge the Council faces.' The strategy includes significant asset rationalisation, reorganisation, and consolidation in communities, with capital receipts generation to support delivery while reducing costs.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand what financial pressures are driving strategic decisions. The council's own framing of 'the extent of the challenge' signals material financial stress requiring active management through asset sales and consolidation.
findings.figures: No quantification given for the scope of the financial challenge
findings.quote: In November 2024, Cabinet approved the approach and guiding principles of Our Future Council (OFC) in recognition of the extent of the financial challenge the Council faces.

findings.paper_title: Building New and Better Homes - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026-2027 including Rent and Service Charges
findings.headline: Energy efficiency compliance: 50% of stock requires EPC C improvements by 2030 with no HRA funding provision
findings.detail: Government target requires all socially rented homes to achieve EPC C rating by 2030. Around 50% of Wolverhampton's stock requires improvements to meet this. Section 6.11 explicitly states 'There is currently no provision in the HRA to fund the level of investment required' and external funding contributions must be sought.
findings.matters: Creates regulatory risk of future non-compliance with government energy efficiency standards; dependence on external grant funding limits council's control; deferred investment may result in costly emergency compliance spend.
findings.figures: 50% of stock requires improvements; 2030 deadline; no current HRA funding provision
findings.quote: All socially rented homes need to achieve an EPC C by 2030, around 50% of our stock requires improvements to achieve this target. There is currently no provision in the HRA to fund the level of investment required

findings.paper_title: Building New and Better Homes - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026-2027 including Rent and Service Charges
findings.headline: Right to Buy applications surge reduced rental income; housing stock declining despite new build
findings.detail: Stock declining from 21,680 (2022-23 outturn) to projected 21,068 (2025-26), a loss of 612 units over three years. The 2024 Autumn Budget changes to Right to Buy generated a significant surge in applications, reducing rental income to the HRA despite new build and acquisitions programme adding 347 homes.
findings.matters: Reduces rental income base and asset base; net stock loss limits council's capacity to address 8,172-person housing waiting list and constrains revenue for capital investment.
findings.figures: 933 sales over last five years; 347 additional/replacement homes in same period; net loss of 612 units (21,680 to 21,068); 8,172 on waiting list
findings.quote: In 2024, through the Autumn budget, the government announced changes to the Right to Buy scheme which resulted in a significant increase in applications, and although many did not progress to a sale, the surge in applications has led to a reduced rental income to the HRA.

findings.paper_title: Building New and Better Homes - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026-2027 including Rent and Service Charges
findings.headline: 67% of housing stock over 60 years old; significant component replacement backlog with £30,000 average void costs
findings.detail: Approximately 67% of the council's stock is over 60 years old (28% built pre-1944). Following the £314m Decent Homes programme 2007-2015, components including kitchens, bathrooms, heating and electrical systems are reaching end-of-life simultaneously. Average void property costs are around £30,000, impacting lettings pipeline.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance creates long-term asset deterioration risk; ageing components increase reactive repair costs and void periods; failure to invest will erode asset base and rental returns.
findings.figures: 67% over 60 years; 28% pre-1944; £314 million Decent Homes programme 2007-2015; £30,000 average void costs
findings.quote: Approximately 67% of council stock is over 60 years old, with around 28% built before 1944 and therefore requires significant investment or redevelopment

findings.paper_title: Building New and Better Homes - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026-2027 including Rent and Service Charges
findings.headline: Council anticipates difficult decisions on investment levels and service standards to identify savings
findings.detail: Section 7.5-7.6 explicitly anticipates 'difficult decisions will need to be made about levels of investment in our housing stock and service standards, to identify savings and efficiencies.' This suggests planned retrenchment beyond what the 4.8% rent increase alone provides.
findings.matters: Service standard reductions or selective disinvestment would affect tenant satisfaction, regulatory compliance risk, and asset quality; signals management's view that revenue-side decisions cannot fully resolve pressures.
findings.figures: No specific figures quantifying planned reductions
findings.quote: it is anticipated that difficult decisions will need to be made about levels of investment in our housing stock and service standards, to identify savings and efficiencies

findings.paper_title: Building New and Better Homes - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026-2027 including Rent and Service Charges
findings.headline: Current borrowing capacity insufficient for required capital investment; comprehensive capital review needed
findings.detail: Section 6.12 explicitly states that whilst current borrowing levels are sustainable, they are 'not sufficient to continue to invest in our housing at the current/required level.' A comprehensive review of the capital programme will be carried out in 2026-2027 to ensure borrowing remains affordable.
findings.matters: Signals capital investment will be lower than operationally required; constrains ability to deliver new homes (waiting list 8,172), maintain aging stock (67% over 60 years old), or meet regulatory standards.
findings.figures: Capital programme over 10 years projected at £886 million, but level of borrowing cannot support all identified needs
findings.quote: Whilst current levels of borrowing are sustainable to support a certain level of capital investment, that level is not sufficient to continue to invest in our housing at the current/required level.

findings.paper_title: Building New and Better Homes - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026-2027 including Rent and Service Charges
findings.headline: HRA budget pressures requiring comprehensive mid-term review during 2026-2027
findings.detail: The council has explicitly noted that HRA budget pressures will require a comprehensive mid-term review of the Business Plan and medium-term capital and revenue budgets during 2026-2027. This is not routine annual review but signals fundamental affordability challenges.
findings.matters: Mid-term reviews typically precede service reductions, asset disposals, or investment cutbacks; signals that 4.8% rent increase is insufficient to maintain current investment plans.
findings.figures: Review to occur during 2026-2027
findings.quote: due to HRA budget pressures a comprehensive mid-term review of the HRA Business Plan, medium term capital and revenue budgets will be undertaken and reported on during 2026-2027

findings.paper_title: Building New and Better Homes - Housing Revenue Account Business Plan 2026-2027 including Rent and Service Charges
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing inspection outcome due 28 January 2026, following June 2025 self-referral
findings.detail: The Regulator commenced a four-yearly cycle inspection on 4 August 2025. The Regulatory Judgement is due on the same date as this Cabinet meeting (28 January 2026). The self-referral was triggered by assessment that the council did not meet Consumer Standards, particularly around stock condition data.
findings.matters: Regulatory inspection outcomes can result in formal directions, restrictions on service delivery or borrowing, or placement under enhanced scrutiny; outcome is material to council's risk profile.
findings.figures: Inspection commenced 4 August 2025; Regulatory Judgement due 28 January 2026
findings.quote: The Council completed a self–referral to the Regulator of Social Housing on 11 June 2025 due to our assessment that the Council did not meet the expected outcomes of the Consumer Standards.

findings.headline: Stock condition survey target at risk: only 39.15% completed with March 2027 deadline
findings.detail: As of end-December 2025, only 39.15% of the council's ~21,200 properties have been surveyed, despite a regulatory requirement for 100% stock condition data. Funding acceleration through HRA reserves (£1.0m in 2025-26), but timeline to March 2027 is tight. This non-compliance triggered a self-referral to the Regulator in June 2025.
findings.matters: Failure to meet the March 2027 deadline would constitute ongoing regulatory non-compliance; the council may face enforcement action, directions, or restrictions on borrowing and operations.
